newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Jungle tin town hopes for salvation in Kabila era.
newsitem.headline: Jungle tin town hopes for salvation in Kabila era.

text.p: The jungle is starting to reclaim the tin-mining town of Lulingu in the east of Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of Congo.

Encroaching vegetation is invading brick buildings dating back to before independence from Belgium in 1960, but Kabila's victory and the end of three decades of corrupt and chaotic rule by dictator Mobutu Sese Seko have fuelled hopes of change.
"We want roads and communications. We want clean hospitals and schools. We want our nurses to be paid and our teachers to have their salaries," said poultry farmer Tonton Bamalungu.
"Political parties don't do anything. We didn't see Mobutu. We don't see Kabila. But we want to see actions and we want to see change."
Like hundreds of other towns in the former Zaire, isolated and enveloped by forest, Lulingu was largely forgotten under Mobutu. Only its tin mine saved it from total abandonment.
Since the 1980s, tin prices on the world market have dropped and mud roads to the town have crumbled, making it costly and time-consuming to export the tin.
Lulingu, 150 km east of Bukavu, the provincial capital of South Kivu, escaped largely unscathed in the civil war.
Inhabitants say they saw different armies pass through and refugees swamp their hospital, but they escaped the looting and bloodshed elsewhere in the region.
"We lived through the events, but we weren't touched," said Tonton Bamalungu.
Kabila has banned political activity in the far-away capital Kinshasa but has promised to rebuild the country's shattered infrastructure and improve the lot of its 45 million people.

Politicial analysts say that if he can harness the country's vast mineral and agricultural wealth and plough it into redevelopment, he may neutralise any discontent over the initial autocracy of his new regime.
It has been three years since the small team of teachers and officials in Lulingu saw a regular salary. Impoverished residents had to contribute to hospital and education costs.
The 500 manual labourers and other staff of the part-Belgian, part state-owned SOMINKI (Societe Miniere et Industrielle du Kivu) tin mine have had no pay since February.
Expatriate staff fled the town when war approached last year.
Government figures for nationwide tin production show a drop from 3,334 tonnes in 1986 to 793 in 1994. The future of tin mining in the new Congo is far from assured.
During years in which world prices for the metal dropped, the semi-industrial mines at Lulingu were in part subsidized by the gold mines SOMINKI ran in nearby Kamituga.
But those too have been abandoned since they were heavily looted and vandalised last year by passing soldiers of Mobutu's defeated army and allied Hutu militias from Burundi.

Today, the solid brick buildings of the 200-bed hospital equipped with laboratory and operating theatre, the huge garages for SOMINKI trucks, and the many brick houses built in pre-independence times risk being overrun by jungle.
Rumours have spread that potential buyers could be coming. Should they arrive, the inhabitants may escape a gruelling life of subsistence.
But not all Lulingu's 6,000 inhabitants are optimistic.
"The old authorities did not visit us. They forgot us. We are now in a period of observation, but there is no sign yet we will be remembered," said a local doctor.
